source.title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing

accepted.question_text: In randomized wait-free consensus for an asynchronous shared-memory system of n processes, where consensus requires agreement, validity, and eventual decision, and where wait-freedom means that every process terminates in finitely many of its own steps regardless of scheduling, what is the optimal expected register-operation complexity under an adaptive adversary that knows the current system state? In particular, can the known O(n^2 log n) expected total-work protocol using atomic read-write registers, or O(n^2) expected total-work protocol using counters, be improved using objects constructible from atomic registers, or can the lower bound be raised to show that quadratic work is necessary?

evidence.quote: The open question that then arises is the complexity of solving consensus, measured by the expected number of register operations carried out by all processes (total work) or by any one process (per-process work).
A faster protocol would thus require a significantly new approach. Conversely, an Omega(n^2) lower bound would show that voting is optimal.

accepted.question_text: For randomized wait-free consensus against a weak adversary that cannot observe private coin flips before they are made public, where an O(log n) per-process work protocol is known using multi-writer registers, can one prove a nontrivial lower bound, ideally an Omega(log n) lower bound, for multi-writer registers or even for stronger objects such as unit-cost snapshots?

evidence.quote: With a weaker adversary that cannot observe coin flips that have not yet been made public, consensus can be solved in O(log n) work per process using multi-writer registers [11]. There is no corresponding non-trivial lower bound.
It would be interesting to see if an Omega(log n) lower bound could be proved for multi-writer registers or even with strong objects like unit-cost snapshots.

accepted.question_text: In oblivious routing on a graph-modeled multi-hop network, where each newly injected packet chooses a path independently of the path choices of other packets, congestion is the maximum number of selected paths using any edge, and stretch is the ratio between the selected path length and the shortest-path length, for which network classes or structural circumstances can an oblivious routing algorithm simultaneously achieve near-optimal congestion and small, ideally constant, stretch?

evidence.quote: An interesting open problem is to examine the circumstances in which congestion and stretch can be optimized simultaneously.
A second interesting open problem is to find other classes of networks where the congestion and stretch are minimized simultaneously.

accepted.question_text: In oblivious routing, let C be congestion and D be the maximum path length produced by the routing. Which classes of networks admit oblivious routing algorithms for which C + D is close to the offline optimum, so that packet delivery can be scheduled in time proportional to C + D?
accepted.context_brief: Oblivious routing C plus D objective

evidence.quote: Another interesting open problem is to find classes of networks in which oblivious routing gives C + D close to the off-line optimal, where C is the congestion and D is the maximum path length.

accepted.question_text: For ongoing self-stabilizing consensus, where a sequence of consensus instances has input vectors and output values over time, and where stability means changing the output as few times as possible when successive input vectors allow the previous output to remain valid, what is the most stable consensus function when the only validity restriction is that the common output must equal at least t + 1 process inputs?

evidence.quote: Namely, we would like to minimize the number of times the output is changed.
The open problem is, to determine the most stable (consensus) function to use, given flexibility in deciding on the output of the system.
assuming that the function from the inputs to the common output is only restricted to ensure that the output has a value equal to at least t + 1 inputs.

accepted.question_text: For memoryless symmetric ongoing consensus functions, where the function output is invariant under permutations of input positions, how can the approximately factor-2 gap between known upper and lower bounds on the number of output changes be closed, and how should non-geodesic input-change paths be analyzed to distinguish and evaluate the performance of different consensus functions?
accepted.context_brief: Stability bounds for memoryless symmetric consensus

evidence.quote: An upper bound for the number of output changes for a memoryless symmetric system (where the function has the same output regardless of the position of inputs in the input vector) is presented in [20].
Closing this gap, as well as considering non geodesic input path changes that are useful to separate the performance and to evaluate consensus functions are open questions.

accepted.question_text: For multi-valued ongoing consensus, where inputs and outputs need not be binary and the required output may be any value lying within the range of the correct input values, which consensus functions should be explored to optimize stability, meaning to minimize output changes over time while preserving the stated validity condition?

evidence.quote: Multi-valued consensus extends the case of binary-valued consensus, allowing the inputs (and the output) to be a non-necessarily binary value.
Also in the case of multi-valued consensus one may only require an output value that is within the range of values of the correct values, further exploring functions is also open.

accepted.question_text: For wait-free linearizable implementations of an m-component atomic snapshot object from shared registers, where SCAN returns a consistent view of all components and UPDATE changes one component, what are the tight space-time tradeoffs for SCAN time beyond the known space-optimal lower bound and the best known upper bounds? In particular, can the gap between existing lower bounds for implementations using a fixed number of registers and the known O(n)-time implementations using many or unbounded registers be closed?

evidence.quote: A snapshot implementation from registers uses shared registers to simulate the snapshot components and provides algorithms for SCAN and UPDATE.
Bridging the gap between the lower bounds provided in [29] and the best known upper bounds (discussed above) is a challenging open problem.

accepted.question_text: For wait-free linearizable register implementations of multi-writer atomic snapshot objects with m components and n processes, what is the optimal time complexity of UPDATE? More specifically, can one prove UPDATE lower bounds stronger than the known Omega(m) bound, or design implementations with UPDATE time better than the known O(n) bound?

evidence.quote: Since the best known snapshot implementation [8] has time complexity O(n) for UPDATE, it is unknown if this lower bound is optimal.
Proving better lower bounds for the time complexity of UPDATE or designing more efficient algorithms (in terms of the UPDATE time complexity) is an intriguing open problem.

accepted.question_text: For wait-free linearizable register implementations of atomic snapshot objects, what are the full tradeoffs among the number of registers used, the worst-case time complexity of SCAN operations, and the worst-case time complexity of UPDATE operations?

evidence.quote: The identification of tradeoffs between the number of registers used in an implementation, the time complexity of SCAN, and the time complexity of UPDATE is another interesting open problem.

accepted.question_text: Can randomization be used to obtain efficient implementations of multi-writer atomic snapshot objects from registers, potentially beating deterministic lower bounds on snapshot space-time tradeoffs?

evidence.quote: The lower bounds proved in [28, 29] hold for deterministic algorithms and they can be possibly beaten by employing randomization.
Finding efficient randomized implementations for multi-writer snapshot objects remains a challenging open problem.

accepted.question_text: In the incomplete-information extension of the KP selfish-routing model, where n selfish users route unsplittable traffic over m parallel links, links may have several possible capacities, and each user's belief about link capacities is a probability distribution that may differ from the beliefs of other users, does every instance admit a Pure Nash Equilibrium, or can the conjecture that such equilibria always exist be disproved?
accepted.context_brief: Pure Nash equilibria with link-capacity beliefs

evidence.quote: The problem of existence of pure Nash Equilibria for this new model in the general case is a non-trivial problem; as of this writing, it remains open.
It is conjectured that the model introduced in [38] always admits a Pure Nash equilibrium in general. Proving or disproving this conjecture is an interesting open challenge.

accepted.question_text: For the asynchronous deterministic shared-memory Write-All problem, where p processors must write to t distinct memory locations while an adaptive adversary may introduce dynamic processor failures or delays and work counts all processor steps, can one either prove a work lower bound stronger than Omega(t log t) or design an asynchronous algorithm for the case p = t whose work is asymptotically less than O(t^(1+epsilon)) for every fixed epsilon > 0?

evidence.quote: Write-All, formulated in terms of p processors writing to t distinct memory locations in the presence of an adaptive adversary that introduces dynamic failures or delays.

Thus we formulate our first, two-pronged, open problem as follows: (a) can a stronger than Omega(t log t) lower bound on work be shown for asynchronus Write-All problem, and/or (b) is there an algorithm for asynchronous processors that solves the problem with work asymptotically less than O(t^(1+epsilon)) for p = t?

accepted.question_text: For the asynchronous deterministic shared-memory Write-All problem with p processors and t memory locations under adversarial failures or delays, is it possible to achieve optimal total work O(t) while using p = t^delta processors for some delta greater than 1/2?

evidence.quote: Next observe that an optimal algorithm for Write-All must have work Theta(t).
Our second and final open problem is as follows: Is it possible to solve the asynchronous Write-All problem with optimal work O(t) using the number of processors p = t^delta for delta > 1/2?

accepted.question_text: In a synchronous distributed message-passing network of n nodes, where each node can send O(log n) bits to each neighbor per round and has a distinct O(log n)-bit identifier, what is the distributed round complexity of obtaining a good approximation for a general integer linear program? The general ILP setting includes n producing nodes choosing integer variables x_i, m accepting nodes with constraints of the form sum_i a_{j,i} x_i <= b_j for integer coefficients, and an objective to minimize or approximate sum_i c_i x_i, without assuming that the coefficients form a metric.

evidence.quote: The distributed complexity (i.e. number of rounds to achieve a good approximation) of the general integer-linear programs is a major open problem.
We want here a small number of rounds (constant number would be fine). Note that we do not assume that the a_i_j form a metric. They can also be arbitrarily large.

accepted.question_text: In a distributed Stackelberg-style selfish routing problem, where each node i wants to send flow x_i to a destination, the total flow is r, a subset L of non-selfish nodes can coordinate under a leader, and the remaining nodes selfishly route their flows to avoid high delay, can one find distributed algorithms by which the nodes in L choose their flows so that the Nash Equilibrium reached by the selfish nodes is close to an optimal flow routing such as minimum total latency?

evidence.quote: Some of the nodes (belonging to a subset L) are not selfish but they agree to work together (e.g. under an elected leader). The rest route their flows selfishly to avoid big delays.
Finding distributed solutions to the selfish optimization problem described above, remains an open problem

accepted.question_text: In the k-local distributed algorithm model, where each node can communicate with its neighbors at most k times and therefore can gather only information from its k-neighborhood, is there a deterministic local construction of a maximal independent set in general graphs, and what local complexity can such a construction achieve?

evidence.quote: In a k-local algorithm, for some parameter k, each node can communicate at most k times with its neighbors.
There have been recent advances on both upper [51] and lower [50] bounds; however, many basic questions (e.g. a deterministic local construction of a maximal independent set) are still open.

accepted.question_text: For geometric graph models motivated by wireless sensor networks, especially unit disk graphs where geometry constrains node placement and wireless links, what is the local complexity of typical coordination tasks such as computing a dominating set under k-local communication?
accepted.context_brief: Local algorithms on unit disk graphs

evidence.quote: So far, very little is known about local algorithms for geometric graphs.
To give a specific example, even for a simple model known as unit disk graph, the local complexity of typical coordination tasks (e.g., computing a dominating set) is an open problem.

trace.notes: Normalized the input as a zbMATH bibliographic resolver URL with trailing identifier 5605099.

Local fetch of the zbMATH landing page returned HTTP 403, but the zbMATH API resolved identifier 5605099 to the journal article titled 'Eight open problems in distributed computing.' in Bulletin of the European Association for Theoretical Computer Science EATCS 90, pages 109-126, 2006.

Exact-title recovery found James Aspnes's publication page and its PDF link. The PDF title and bibliography matched the zbMATH metadata. Shell curl to the Yale PDF failed with DNS resolution from the sandbox, so extraction used the readable PDF URL exposed by the page-reading tool.

Mapped the PDF title page, abstract, eight numbered sections, and references. The likely open-problem regions are sections 1 through 8: Wait-Free Consensus; Oblivious Routing; Stability of Continuous Consensus; Complexity of Implementing Atomic Snapshots; Pure Nash Equilibria in Selfish Routing; Adverse Cooperative Computing; Distributed Approximations; and Sensor Networks: Locality for Geometric Graphs.
Extracted two wait-free consensus candidates: adaptive-adversary expected work and weak-adversary lower bounds.
Extracted oblivious-routing candidates about simultaneous congestion/stretch optimization and the C + D objective.
Extracted continuous-consensus candidates about the most stable function, memoryless symmetric bounds and non-geodesic paths, and multi-valued consensus.
Extracted four atomic-snapshot candidates: SCAN space-time bounds, UPDATE complexity, three-way register/SCAN/UPDATE tradeoffs, and randomized multi-writer snapshots.
Extracted the Pure Nash Equilibrium existence/conjecture candidate for selfish routing with incomplete link-capacity information.
Extracted two asynchronous Write-All candidates: the large work gap for p = t and optimal O(t) work with p = t^delta, delta > 1/2.
Extracted two distributed-approximation candidates: general ILP round complexity and distributed Stackelberg-style selfish optimization.
Extracted two local-algorithm candidates: deterministic local maximal independent set construction and local complexity of coordination tasks on unit disk graphs.
Merged two overlapping oblivious-routing formulations about simultaneous congestion and stretch optimization into q_003. All other candidates were retained as distinct research questions.

Accepted q_001 through q_018. Each accepted item has a self-contained rewrite, page-numbered PDF evidence, no source-pointing language in question_text, and is_solved=false because the source does not mark any item solved.
Saved exact JSON output to outputs/parse-paper/5605099.json and outputs/latest.json.
